olympiad_full_name: United States of America Mathematical Olympiad
statement:
Find all integers
$$n\ge3$$
such that the following property holds: if we list the divisors of $n!$ in increasing order as
$$1=d_1<d_2<\cdots<d_k=n!,$$
then we have
$$d_2-d_1\le d_3-d_2\le\cdots\le d_k-d_{k-1}.$$
statement_note: Divisor-ordering notation visually verified from official PDF because OCR partially corrupted subscripts and inequalities. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}

olympiad_full_name: United States of America Mathematical Olympiad
statement:
Let
$$S_1,S_2,\ldots,S_{100}$$
be finite sets of integers whose intersection is not empty. For each nonempty subset
$$T\subseteq\{S_1,S_2,\ldots,S_{100}\},$$
the size of the intersection of the sets in $T$ is a multiple of the number of sets in $T$. What is the least possible number of elements that are in at least $50$ sets?

olympiad_full_name: United States of America Mathematical Olympiad
statement:
Let $m$ be a positive integer. A triangulation of a polygon is called $m$-balanced if its triangles can be colored with $m$ colors in such a way that the sum of the areas of all triangles of the same color is the same for each of the $m$ colors. Find all positive integers $n$ for which there exists an $m$-balanced triangulation of a regular $n$-gon.

Note: A triangulation of a convex polygon $P$ with $n\ge3$ sides is any partitioning of $P$ into $n-2$ triangles by $n-3$ diagonals of $P$ that do not intersect in the polygon’s interior.
figure_description: Balanced colorings of triangulations of a regular polygon.
statement_note: The OCR contained broken forum markup around 'm-balanced'; wording was visually corrected from the PDF. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}

olympiad_full_name: United States of America Mathematical Olympiad
statement: Let $m$ and $n$ be positive integers. A circular necklace contains $mn$ beads, each either red or blue. It turns out that no matter how the necklace is cut into $m$ blocks of $n$ consecutive beads, each block has a distinct number of red beads. Determine, with proof, all possible ordered pairs $(m,n)$.
figure_description: Circular necklace partitioned into consecutive blocks with distinct red-bead counts.

olympiad_full_name: United States of America Mathematical Olympiad
statement:
Point $D$ is selected inside acute triangle $ABC$ so that
$$\angle DAC=\angle ACB$$
and
$$\angle BDC=90^\circ+\angle BAC.$$
Point $E$ is chosen on ray $BD$ so that
$$AE=EC.$$
Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Show that line $AB$ is tangent to the circumcircle of triangle $BEM$.
figure_description: Acute triangle with interior point and tangent circumcircle condition.
statement_note: Right-angle expression visually verified from official PDF because OCR partially corrupted the degree symbol. :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}

olympiad_full_name: United States of America Mathematical Olympiad
statement:
Let $n>2$ be an integer and let
$$\ell\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}.$$
A collection
$$A_1,\ldots,A_k$$
of (not necessarily distinct) subsets of
$$\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$$
is called $\ell$-large if
$$|A_i|\ge\ell$$
for all
$$1\le i\le k.$$
Find, in terms of $n$ and $\ell$, the largest real number $c$ such that the inequality
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k}
 x_ix_j
 \frac{|A_i\cap A_j|^2}{|A_i|\cdot|A_j|}
\ge
c\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k}x_i\right)^2
$$
holds for all positive integers $k$, all nonnegative real numbers
$$x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_k,$$
and all $\ell$-large collections
$$A_1,A_2,\ldots,A_k$$
of subsets of
$$\{1,2,\ldots,n\}.$$
figure_description: Intersection-density inequality for collections of subsets.
statement_note: Double summation and fraction structure carefully reconstructed from the official PDF because OCR partially corrupted the inequality layout. :contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3}
